---
# On the Slow Work of Noticing

I am sitting on the porch of a rented cabin in the Catskills, and the morning is doing something unspeakably ordinary: it is arriving. The light has not yet cleared the ridge, so the valley below is a bowl of gray-blue mist, and the grass is wet in a way that only grass can be wet before the sun has had a chance to argue with it. There is a bird—I cannot name it, though I should be able to—repeating the same three notes over and over, as if it is testing the quality of the air. The coffee in my hands is hot. There is no hurry.

I have not written freely like this in a long time. Not because I lack words, but because I have come to distrust the conditions under which words are usually produced. Most of my writing these days is squeezed into small gaps between notifications, or built out of fragments harvested while waiting for a meeting to start, or typed while half-listening to a podcast about the end of the world. The writing that matters—the kind that changes you, that makes you look up from the page as if you had just realized you were being watched—requires a different kind of climate. It requires boredom, slowness, a willingness to sit with the blankness of the page until the page stops being blank. It requires, in short, the thing that the modern world has made almost impossible: a sustained period of undirected attention.

This is what I have been trying to think about, in the loose and undistinguished way that one thinks about things before one is ready to write them: attention. Not the kind of attention that is measured by analytics, or the kind that is bought and sold by advertisers, or the kind that is constantly being optimized and gamified by the designers of the apps we are ashamed to be scrolling through. I mean the older, slower, more dangerous kind. The kind that is almost indistinguishable from love. The kind that, when you give it to something, you are quietly saying: you are worthy of my time, and time is the only thing I truly have.

There is a phrase often attributed to the French philosopher Simone Weil, though it is more of a distillation than a direct quote: “Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.” I used to read that as a nice sentiment, a bit of mystical wisdom to be admired and then put aside. Now I think it is one of the most profound and practically important statements that has ever been made about how to live. Because attention is not just a cognitive act. It is not merely a matter of directing your eyes or your ears toward something. It is a moral act. It is a way of allowing the world to be real outside of your own need for it. When you pay attention to a person, you are not just listening to their words; you are creating a space in which their existence becomes undeniable. When you pay attention to a landscape, you are not just looking at it; you are entering into a relationship with it, one in which you are not the center.

And when you pay attention to a single, small, seemingly insignificant thing—a bird repeating three notes, a blade of grass, the particular way the light falls on a wooden table—you are doing something quietly revolutionary. You are resisting the pull of the abstract, the spectacular, the catastrophic. You are saying that the world is not just a set of data points to be processed and discarded, but a dense, textured, infinite field of meaning. You are saying that the small is not the enemy of the large, but its foundation.

# II

I did not come to these thoughts by accident. I came to them by walking.

A few years ago, I moved to a new city, and I began a practice that I have kept ever since: I started walking the same route every morning, at the same time, regardless of weather. The route is not long—about two miles, down a residential street, past a small park, across a bridge over a creek, and then back along a different road. It is not a scenic route, strictly speaking. There is no dramatic vista, no ocean, no mountain range. Just houses, lawns, cars, a few trees, a gas station, a convenience store, and the creek, which in the dry season is little more than a trickle of mud and stones.

At first, the walk was boring. I would put in earbuds and listen to something—a book, a podcast, a playlist—to fill the silence. But after a while, the earbuds began to irritate me, and I took them out. And what I discovered was that the walk was not actually boring at all. It was just that I had never bothered to look at it.

The first thing I noticed was the dogs. There is a golden retriever who lives in the blue house on the corner, and every morning she is standing at the gate, watching the street with the serene patience of a creature who has never once questioned the usefulness of her own existence. There is a small, wiry terrier who is walked by an old man in a flannel shirt, and the terrier stops at exactly the same fire hydrant every day, sniffs it for precisely eleven seconds, and then moves on. There is a black lab who has learned to lie in the sun on the driveway of the house with the red door, and when I pass by, he lifts his head and looks at me with an expression that seems to say: *If you were me, you would not be in such a hurry.*

Then I noticed the plants. There is a particular hedge of azaleas that blooms in mid-May, and one year I watched it go from tight green buds to a riot of pink in the span of a single week. There is a magnolia tree in the park that loses its leaves all at once in the autumn, and the sound of the leaves hitting the ground is like the sound of a great hand gently exhaling. There is a patch of wild mint that grows along the creek, and when I crush a leaf between my fingers, the smell is so sharp and clean that it feels like a memory of something I have never experienced.

And then I noticed the light. The way it changes, not just from season to season, but from day to day, minute to minute. Sometimes the morning light is pale and watery, as if the world were being viewed through the bottom of a glass. Sometimes it is golden and thick, like honey being poured over the rooftops. Sometimes it is gray and flat, and the houses look like they are carved from the same stone as the sky. I began to understand that the walk was never really the same walk. It was always a new walk, wearing the clothes of the old one. And the only reason it had seemed repetitive was that I had not been paying attention.

This is the first lesson of the slow work of noticing: repetition is not monotony. It is invitation. The same route, walked a hundred times, is a hundred different routes. But you can only see the difference if you are willing to be bored, to be empty, to let the world speak instead of always trying to speak at it.

# III

There is a reason why the digital economy is built on the destruction of this capacity. Attention is the raw material of almost everything in our age—advertising, politics, culture, even friendship. And the most reliable way to extract value from attention is to fragment it, to keep it moving, to never allow it to settle. The scroll is the perfect technology for this. It presents an infinite series of small, novel, mildly interesting things, none of which requires more than a moment of engagement. The scroll is not a tool for reading. It is a tool for avoiding the possibility of reading, for avoiding the possibility of any sustained encounter with a single thing that might demand something from you.

I have spent hours of my life scrolling. I have spent hours of my life watching videos that I do not remember, reading articles that I could not summarize, absorbing information that vanished from my mind the moment it entered it. And I have noticed, in myself, a strange new symptom: the inability to sit with a thought without immediately reaching for my phone. It is not that I have something to say or something to check. It is that the silence of my own mind has become uncomfortable. It is that the sensation of having only my own thoughts for company feels like a kind of withdrawal.

This is not a new insight. Every critic of the modern age, from Nicholas Carr to Jenny Odell to Mary Oliver, has pointed out the same thing. But the insight bears repeating, because the experience does not get less urgent, the more it is described. There is a kind of poverty that is invisible to the people who suffer from it, and that poverty is the poverty of attention. You can have a full bank account, a full refrigerator, a full calendar, and still be starving—starving for silence, starving for depth, starving for the feeling of being fully present in a single moment, in a single place, with a single other being.

The strange thing is that the tools that promised to connect us have made us less capable of connection. Because connection requires attention, and attention requires time, and time requires the willingness to let a relationship unfold at its own pace, without interruption, without optimization, without the constant sense that there might be something better, shinier, more immediate just around the corner. When you are with someone and you are checking your phone, you are not really with them. You are with the phone, and the phone is with everyone else. And the person in front of you knows it—not always consciously, but in the way that a plant knows the direction of the light. They know that they are only partially receiving your attention, and that partial attention is not the same as attention. It is the shadow of attention. It is attention with one foot out the door.

# IV

I have often wondered whether the slow work of noticing can be taught, or whether it is just a temperament that some people have and others do not. I have come to believe that it is a practice, not a personality trait. And like all practices, it requires a kind of discipline—but not the discipline of forcing yourself to do something you hate. The discipline of removing the obstacles that prevent you from doing what you love. The discipline of putting the phone in another room. The discipline of taking the earbuds out. The discipline of walking the same route and not getting bored. The discipline of being with your own thoughts even when they are not interesting, because it is only in the boring, empty, unfocused spaces that interesting thoughts have room to grow.

I wonder if this is why so many of my best ideas have come to me in the shower, or while washing dishes, or while doing some other repetitive, mindless task. It is not because the shower is a magical place. It is because the shower is one of the few remaining places where I am not being stimulated, where my attention is not being captured, where my mind is free to wander. And a wandering mind is not a wasted mind. A wandering mind is a mind that is making connections, that is sorting memories, that is weaving together disparate threads into new patterns. The problem with the constant stimulus of the digital world is not that it fills our minds with bad content. It is that it fills our minds with any content at all. It leaves no room for the spontaneous, the unexpected, the unbidden. It leaves no room for surprise.

The slow work of noticing is the work of making room for surprise. It is the work of going to the same place every day and letting that place become new. It is the work of reading a single poem ten times and discovering, on the tenth reading, that you had never really read it before. It is the work of sitting with a person you love and not checking your phone, not because you are trying to be good, but because you have realized that the phone is a thief, and you have decided that you do not want to be robbed anymore.

# V

There is a specific kind of attention that I want to practice, and it is the kind that is directed at the non-human world. I have been walking the same route for years, and I have come to know it the way that one knows an old friend—not just its broad outlines, but its moods, its quirks, its small daily changes. I know which house puts out a Christmas wreath in early November and leaves it up until March. I know which dog barks at the mailman and which one just watches silently. I know where the sidewalk is cracked and where the roots of the maple tree have lifted the pavement. I know when the light hits the window of the yellow house at a certain angle, and the whole house glows like it is made of amber.

This knowledge is useless in any economic sense. It cannot be monetized. It cannot be turned into a metric or a bullet point on a resume. It is a kind of knowledge that is valuable simply because it makes the world more real. When you know a place this intimately, you cannot treat it as a backdrop for your own drama. You cannot see it as just a scenery, just a resource, just a place to get from A to B. It becomes a presence, an organism, a community of living things of which you are a part. And this, I think, is the deepest purpose of attention: not to master the world, but to be in relationship with it. To notice the crow that sits on the same telephone wire every afternoon, and to wonder, briefly, what it is thinking. To notice the first frost on the grass, and to feel not just the cold, but the passage of time. To notice the way the creek changes after a rain, swollen and brown and impatient, and to understand that you are living in a world that is always moving, always changing, always becoming something other than what it was.

In one of her notebooks, the poet Mary Oliver wrote: “Attention is the beginning of devotion.” I think this is exactly right. Devotion is usually imagined as a grand, sweeping thing—a commitment to a cause, a person, a god. But the most enduring devotions are built out of small, repeated acts of attention. The daily walk. The daily prayer. The daily practice of sitting down at the desk and writing, even when you have nothing to say. The daily choice to look at the person you love and actually see them. These are the bricks of a life. And if you do not pay attention to the bricks, the life will be hollow, no matter how grand its architecture.

# VI

I have been writing this essay for several days now, and I have noticed that the act of writing about attention has changed the way I pay attention. I am more aware of the texture of things. The grain of the wood on this desk. The sound of the refrigerator humming in the next room. The weight of the coffee cup in my hand. I am more aware of the time, of the way it passes, of the fact that I will not live forever, and that every moment I spend not paying attention is a moment I have spent as if I were already dead.

This is the terrifying thing about the slow work of noticing: it forces you to confront the fact that your life is finite. If you are constantly distracted, constantly skimming the surface of experience, you can avoid this confrontation. You can pretend that there will always be more time, more chances, more moments. But when you slow down and pay attention, you realize that each moment is irreplaceable. This particular morning, with this particular light, this particular bird, this particular silence—it will never happen again. And the only way to honor it is to be present for it, to let it in, to allow it to become part of you.

There is a line from the poet Rainer Maria Rilke that I have carried with me for years, from his *Letters to a Young Poet*: “Have patience with everything unresolved in your heart and try to love the questions themselves.” I used to think of this as good advice for a young person, for someone who was struggling with uncertainty. But now I think it is also good advice for the practice of attention. The world is full of questions. Why does the light do that? Why does the bird sing those three notes? Why does this moment feel so full, so heavy, so significant, when nothing is happening at all? You do not need to answer them. You just need to let them be, to sit with them, to let them deepen. The answer, if there is one, will come in its own time. Or it will not. And that is also fine.

# VII

It is now late afternoon. The light has shifted again, and the valley is no longer full of mist. The bird is gone, or has fallen silent. The coffee is long since finished. I have been sitting here for hours, doing nothing in particular, and I have come to a strange conclusion: this is the work. This is the real work. Not the writing, not the thinking, not the producing of something that can be measured or shared or consumed. The real work is the paying attention. The writing is just a byproduct, a way of recording the attention, of making it last a little longer.

I think about the people who will read this, if anyone does. I hope they will not read it as a set of instructions. I hope they will not read it as a criticism of their own habits, a judgment of their own distractedness. I hope they will read it as an invitation. An invitation to take a walk without your phone. An invitation to sit in silence for five minutes and see what comes. An invitation to notice the small things, the overlooked things, the things that seem too ordinary to be worth your time. Because they are not too ordinary. They are the only things that are real.

The world is enormous, and it is mostly made of tiny, unremarkable things. A blade of grass. A drop of water. A single note from a bird. The way a stranger’s face changes when they smile. These are not distractions from the important work of life. They are the important work. They are the texture of existence, the very fabric of being. And the slow work of noticing is the work of weaving yourself into that fabric, of becoming a part of it, of understanding that you are not a separate observer but a participant, a thread, a small and temporary piece of a vast and ancient pattern.

I am going to go for another walk now. The same route as always. The same street, the same houses, the same creek, the same dogs, the same trees. And I know, with a certainty that I cannot explain, that it will not be the same at all.
---

## Grounded reading
The voice is meditative and earnest, moving from close sensory observation toward broad moral claims. Its pathos comes from treating distraction not merely as an inconvenience but as a way of missing one’s finite life and failing to be present with other people and the non-human world. The repeated walks, birds, dogs, changing light, and creek give the essay a lived-in texture; its invitation to the reader is gentle rather than scolding: make room for quiet, and let ordinary things become particular.

## What the model chose to foreground

It repeatedly returns to ordinary sensory particulars—the bird’s three notes, the route walked each morning, the dogs and plants—as evidence that repetition can become discovery. The essay also emphasizes mortality: noticing matters because each moment is unrepeatable.

## Evidence line
> The world is enormous, and it is mostly made of tiny, unremarkable things.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay coherently develops and repeatedly returns to its central moral emphasis, though its polished public-essay style relies on familiar themes of attention, technology, and presence.
